title: A life by conditions
hook: from conception to awakening, a whole life traced by causes

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sati's mistake, and your line, from conditions. Today, the end of a week, and the same discourse, zoomed all the way out.

Baby photos are strange things. There you are, a few days old, red-faced and furious, and somehow that's you. Then a kid on a tricycle. Then a teenager with that haircut. The album asks a question without saying it: how did that one become this one? Near the end of yesterday's discourse, the Buddha answers it. He walks through an entire human life, from before birth to freedom, and shows each step resting on the one before.
screen: `A BABY PHOTO. A TRICYCLE. THAT HAIRCUT.` → `HOW DID THAT ONE BECOME THIS ONE?` → `A WHOLE LIFE, STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: The second half of the thirty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings begins before birth. A life begins, the text says, when three things come together: the mother and father unite, the mother is in season, and a being to be born is present. Not one condition, three. Then the mother carries the child nine or ten months, with great anxiety, and nourishes it after birth with her own milk; in this teaching, the discourse says, mother's milk is called blood. The child grows, and the text lists children's games: toy plows, little carts, bows and arrows, somersaults, a game with sticks. Then the adult, enjoying the five kinds of sense pleasure. Seeing a pleasant sight, they lean toward it; an unpleasant one, they lean away. Feeling becomes delight, delight becomes clinging, clinging becomes being, and on rolls the wheel of birth, aging and death. Then the turn. A Buddha appears in the world. The person hears the teaching, gains trust, and trains: virtue, guarding the senses, mindfulness, stillness. Now, seeing a sight, they don't lean. Feeling arises, and no delight hooks it. Without delight, no clinging. Without clinging, the wheel stops. Every stage, the baby, the child, the craving adult and the free one, comes from conditions. That's the hope in it. If the knot was tied by causes, it can be untied by causes. And the week looks back: a grove lit many ways, a cowherd's craft, a debater's sweat, a childhood tree, a trembling palace, a fire and its fuel.
screen: `THREE THINGS, AND A LIFE BEGINS` · `CHILDHOOD GAMES, THEN SENSE PLEASURE` · `FEELING, DELIGHT, CLINGING, BIRTH` · `THE TURN: NO DELIGHT, NO CLINGING` · then, large: `ALL FROM CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Pick something real that happened to you, a move, a friendship, a job, a loss, and look for three or four of its causes: a person you met, a choice you made, something that happened before you were born. See how none of them alone was enough, then let it all settle back into the breath, which comes from conditions too.
paticca samuppada. From conception to childhood, craving and freedom, every stage resting on causes, so every knot can be untied.
Your line: all from conditions. Even someone who frustrates you was once a baby with games and hungers. A week, complete.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers present dependent origination (paticca samuppada) as a chain of conditions, painted in Tibetan temple art as the wheel of life; MN 38 gives it as a human life, from conception and childhood to the release that comes when craving ends.

fork.setup: you've heard the teaching and trained. you see a beautiful sight, and a pleasant feeling arises. according to MN 38, what happens next for the trained one?
options: the feeling arises, but no delight hooks it.
nothing: they no longer see sights.
fork.reveal: the trained one still sees and feels. what changes is that delight doesn't seize the feeling, and without delight there's no clinging.

original.note: Pali paticca samuppada: dependent origination, things arising by way of conditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a life is one long thing that just happens to you.
what it means: each stage rests on conditions, which is why the knot of craving can be untied.
what a scholar hears: MN 38 frames the whole life story inside dependent origination, and the discourse's title, the destruction of craving, names what breaks the chain.

chat.says: If everything comes from causes, does that mean we're stuck how we are?
options: No. If the knot was tied by causes, it can be untied by causes.
Yes. Causes set at birth decide everything, and nothing can change them.
No. Causes don't matter; you can become anyone by willpower alone.
chat.meaning: In MN 38 every stage of a life, from conception to freedom, rests on conditions. Without delight, no clinging; without clinging, the wheel stops.

paticca samuppada.meaning: dependent arising: things arising by way of conditions

five kinds of sense pleasure.meaning: the pull of sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches

Middle-Length Sayings.meaning: the Majjhima Nikaya, a collection of the Buddha's discourses

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 38, Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta (the greater discourse on the destruction of craving), later section

notes: MN 38 paraphrased: three conditions for conception (union of parents, mother in season, the gandhabba present: rendered 'a being to be born'), nine or ten months, milk called blood, children's games, sense pleasures, the chain to birth and death, the trained disciple.
